why_two_percent:
Thank you for the question.

We used the 2% importance threshold as a practical rule for removing features with relatively small measured contributions. We wanted a smaller model, but we did not want to prune so aggressively that potentially useful weather information disappeared.

The important point is that 2% was a fixed comparison rule, not a mathematically optimized value. We applied the same cutoff to the LIME-guided Path A and the XGBoost-gain-guided Path B so the two selection methods faced the same numerical rule. That makes the comparison easier to interpret, although their importance percentages are based on different measures.

A different cutoff could retain a different number of features. In fact, the wind-direction feature ddd_x was close to the boundary and crossed it in some LIME seed runs. So I would not claim 2% is universally optimal. Our supported conclusion is narrower: under this stated rule, LIME-guided refinement reduced the feature set while maintaining comparable predictive performance.
contribution:
Thank you for the question. The baseline was already reasonably strong, so our purpose was broader than increasing one test score. We wanted to see whether an explanation method could help us understand and simplify the model, and then compare that workflow fairly with XGBoost's built-in gain importance.

The ablation result is important here. Cyclic encoding alone reached the same hold-out F1 as the full Path A, so we should not say that LIME caused the observed F1 increase. LIME's supported role was diagnostic: it highlighted influential weather features and helped guide a more compact feature set. In the pruning-only experiment, the model went from 22 predictors to 9 while keeping the baseline F1 on the hold-out.

We also checked explanation stability and tested the differences between models. Neither refinement path showed a statistically established predictive advantage. So the main contribution is a careful example of using explainability as feedback for model refinement and interpretation, while being honest about what did and did not improve.
single_station:
Thank you for the question. At this stage, we cannot say that the model would perform equally well in other cities. All observations used in this study came from the Bandung Geophysical Station, WMO 96783, so the fitted model and its feature ranking reflect that station's data.

Another location may have different relationships among humidity, temperature, wind, season, and rainfall. A model trained only on Bandung observations could therefore lose accuracy when moved elsewhere. We did not run that external test in this paper, so any claim of equal performance would go beyond the evidence.

A useful next experiment would be to test the existing model on another station without retraining it. That would show how much transfers directly. We could then retrain or adapt the model with data from that location and compare the result. For now, our performance claim belongs to the Bandung dataset; the LIME-guided refinement procedure itself could be studied elsewhere, but its success there still needs to be demonstrated.
why_lime:
Thank you for the question. We used LIME because we wanted more than one overall importance ranking. LIME let us inspect how the fitted classifier behaved around individual weather days and then summarize which features repeatedly appeared in those explanations.

That diagnostic view drew attention to average relative humidity and the raw day-of-year feature. It helped motivate the revised seasonal encoding and a smaller feature set. Path A used 13 features instead of the baseline's 22, with comparable predictive performance.

The ablation study also tells us where to be careful. Cyclic encoding alone produced the same hold-out F1 as full Path A, so we cannot say LIME itself caused the numerical F1 increase. Its defensible contribution was guiding interpretation and feature refinement. Whether that extra explanation work is worth its computational cost in another setting would need to be evaluated separately.
lime_vs_gain:
Thank you. XGBoost gain importance was the natural comparator precisely because it is already built into the classifier. Gain summarizes how much a feature improves tree splits, whereas LIME examines local prediction behavior through a surrogate around individual cases. Those are different questions.

We used Path B to ask whether the additional LIME workflow offered value beyond the built-in ranking. Both paths used the same chronological split, XGBoost hyperparameters, and 2% selection rule. However, they did not use identical engineered feature pools, so this is not a perfectly isolated comparison of explanation methods.

The results were mixed in an informative way: both paths produced smaller models and small numerical hold-out changes, with no statistically established performance advantage for either. LIME's clearest added value here was as a diagnostic for refinement, rather than a demonstrated superior predictor selector.
why_xgboost:
Thank you for the question. The inputs are daily tabular weather measurements, and XGBoost is a practical tree-ensemble model for this kind of structured data. It can represent nonlinear relationships and interactions without requiring us to define every combination in advance.

For this paper, the key design choice was to hold the selected XGBoost settings fixed across the baseline, LIME-guided Path A, and gain-guided Path B. That made the feature-refinement comparison more interpretable, because a change in score was less likely to come from changing the classifier settings at the same time.

This does not prove XGBoost is the best model for Bandung. We did not benchmark every model family or operational forecast. Our claim is about how these feature sets behaved under one controlled XGBoost setup.
why_binary:
Thank you. We framed the task around a simple next-day decision: will measurable rain occur or not? In this study, a rainy target means next-day rainfall of at least 0.5 millimeters. That gives us a binary label and allows evaluation with precision, recall, F1, and confusion matrices.

Predicting the amount of rainfall would answer a different question. It would require a regression target, different loss and evaluation measures, and probably special attention to extreme events. A yes-or-no classifier cannot tell a user how many millimeters will fall or whether the rain will be hazardous.

So the binary choice was appropriate for the stated research question, but it narrows the practical meaning of the output. We should not present it as a complete rainfall forecast.
threshold_rain:
Thank you for asking. We counted the next day as rainy when measured rainfall reached at least 0.5 millimeters. This separates measurable rain from very light moisture such as dew or trace drizzle and gives one consistent target rule across the experiment.

The threshold is part of the study definition, not a physical boundary at which the atmosphere suddenly changes. If we moved it upward or downward, some days near the boundary would change class. That could alter class prevalence, the confusion matrix, and the apparent performance of each model.

We did not present a sensitivity analysis over several rain-label cutoffs. The safe conclusion is therefore that our reported scores apply to this particular 0.5-millimeter definition; another operational definition should be tested explicitly.
dataset:
Thank you. We used daily observations from the Bandung Geophysical Station, WMO 96783, covering 2010 through 2020. The data came from BMKG through a curated Kaggle repository. The raw table had 3,910 rows.

We removed rows with missing rainfall because rainfall defines the target and some lagged features. That left 3,243 rows, and feature engineering left 3,236 usable rows. These counts matter because the effective sample is smaller than the raw file and because dropping days can affect calendar alignment for a one-day-ahead target.

All performance claims in this paper come from this one station and this processed sample. Before deployment or generalization, we would want to verify the source records and repeat the analysis on other stations and periods.
split:
Thank you. We split the processed observations in chronological order, because a model intended to predict later weather should not train on future dates. The first 3,107 usable rows formed the training portion; the last 129 observed days, from 3 July through 30 December 2020, formed the final hold-out.

We also used expanding-window time-series cross-validation. In each fold, earlier observations trained the model and a later period was used for evaluation. This is more faithful to the forecasting setting than a random shuffle.

The hold-out is still a short period, and our pipeline was not fully nested for every selection and tuning step. So the chronological split protects the basic time order, but it does not eliminate every evaluation limitation.
holdout_small:
Thank you. A 129-day hold-out is useful as a final chronological check, but it is limited for detecting a small performance difference. It spans July to December 2020 and includes only November and December from the rainy season. A change of one or two predictions can visibly move the reported score.

To get a broader view, we added 16 expanding-window validation folds across 2013 to 2020. Their mean F1 scores were very close for the three paths, and paired fold-level tests did not find a significant difference.

That is why I would report Path A's higher hold-out F1 as a numerical observation, not as a proven general improvement. Longer and multi-station testing would give a stronger estimate.
missing_rr:
Thank you for the question. Rainfall, labeled RR, is special because it defines whether the target day is rainy and also feeds some lag-related features. Filling a missing RR value would create an outcome that was not actually observed, so we removed those rows.

For other weather predictors, we used imputation based on training-set statistics. We avoided interpolation across time because that could use later observations to fill an earlier gap.

There is an important consequence: after rainfall-missing days were removed, the next usable row was not always the next calendar day. We disclose that horizon-alignment limitation and check exact next-day subsets. So missing-data handling avoided invented rainfall labels, but it did not leave the study without trade-offs.
horizon_misalignment:
Thank you. The honest answer is no: not every target is exactly the following calendar day. We removed rows with missing rainfall before constructing the target, so a shifted next row can skip one or more calendar dates. About 15% of targets in the cleaned data, and 23.3% in the hold-out, have this issue.

That is a problem for calling every case a strict H+1 forecast. It is different from future-value leakage: the model is not being given the target's future weather measurements as inputs, but the forecast horizon is sometimes longer than one day.

We checked the subset with exact next-calendar-day alignment. The three paths still had no significant pairwise performance difference there. A stronger future pipeline would preserve a calendar index and create the target before dropping missing rows.
leakage:
Thank you. We checked the timing of lagged and rolling predictors: they use current or earlier observations, so those features do not directly contain future weather values. However, that is not the whole leakage question.

The aggregate LIME ranking used hold-out feature values without labels, whereas gain importance was based on training data. Also, tuning and feature selection were not fully repeated inside every cross-validation training fold, and one CV fold overlaps the final hold-out period. These choices can make evaluation less independent than an ideal design.

I would not dismiss those concerns. Our reported scores describe this workflow, with these limitations. In a stronger replication, selection, imputation, and tuning would be fitted only within each training fold, followed by a genuinely untouched final test period.
unequal_paths:
Thank you. The comparison has common elements: both paths use the same data split, selected XGBoost hyperparameters, and 2% feature-selection rule. Those choices reduce some differences between the workflows.

But the feature-engineering steps are not identical. Path A adds three meteorology-derived features and cyclic day-of-year encoding, while Path B adds one humidity-trend feature. If their scores differ, we cannot attribute the entire difference to LIME versus gain importance alone. The ablation is especially informative because cyclic encoding by itself reached the full Path A hold-out F1.

So I would describe this as a comparison of two practical refinement paths, not a perfectly isolated causal test of explanation methods. A follow-up should start both paths from the same candidate-feature pool.
lime_aggregate:
Thank you. LIME starts with a local explanation for one prediction, so we needed a defined aggregation rule before using it for feature selection. We explained all 129 hold-out instances, took the absolute weight for each feature in each explanation, and averaged those values over instances. A feature absent from a local top-ten list received zero for that instance. We then normalized the totals into shares.

This produces a ranking of features that repeatedly appear with large local weights under our LIME setup. It is not a causal effect estimate or a guarantee that a feature would improve the classifier if manipulated.

The use of hold-out feature values in this ranking is also an evaluation limitation. A cleaner design would aggregate explanations only from training data inside each fold before testing the selected features.
lime_stability:
Thank you. Because LIME uses random perturbations, we repeated the aggregate explanation process with ten seeds for the same 129 cases. The baseline ranking had Kendall's W of 0.976. The top five features appeared in the same set across runs, and average relative humidity ranked first every time.

That supports a narrow stability claim: this ranking was consistent across the tested random seeds under the fixed data and configuration. It does not prove that every local coefficient had the same magnitude, or that the surrogate always represented XGBoost faithfully.

We would need a local fidelity analysis and tests under different reference samples or perturbation settings for that stronger claim. I would therefore call the explanations stable in rank, while keeping their validity as a separate question.
humidity:
Thank you. In the baseline aggregate LIME ranking, average relative humidity, RH_avg, accounted for 42.5% of the total absolute explanation weight and ranked first in all ten seed runs. That makes it a prominent feature in the fitted classifier's explanations.

The direction is meteorologically plausible: more humid air is generally closer to saturation, which can be associated with rain conditions. But model importance is not a controlled intervention. It does not prove that changing RH_avg alone would cause rainfall.

Also, the humidity intervals displayed by LIME come from data-driven quartile bins. They should not be presented as universal physical rain thresholds. The safe statement is that humidity was strongly used by this model on this dataset and under this explanation setup.
dewpoint:
Thank you. Dew point and the temperature–dew point spread describe how close the air is to saturation. A smaller spread can indicate moister conditions, so these are meaningful weather representations to test in a rainfall model.

They are calculated from measured temperature and humidity; they are not independent new sensors. In the training data, the spread and average relative humidity were almost perfectly negatively correlated. That means a high ranking for the spread may mostly re-express the humidity information already present.

This matters for interpretation. We should not claim that the engineered feature reveals a separate causal mechanism or independently adds new information simply because LIME ranks it highly. The ablation and redundancy checks are needed to judge its actual value.
cyclic:
Thank you. Raw day-of-year runs from the beginning to the end of the calendar, so a late-December day and an early-January day have distant integer codes even though they are close in the annual cycle. Sine and cosine map the calendar to a circle and preserve that wraparound relationship.

LIME ranked the raw day-of-year feature second, which drew our attention to its representation. We then tested cyclic encoding in Path A. The ablation showed that cyclic encoding alone reached the same hold-out F1, 0.8276, as full Path A.

So the observed hold-out F1 gain is best attributed to the encoding change in this experiment. LIME helped identify a feature worth reconsidering, but it did not independently establish the gain.
ablation:
Thank you. The ablation is central to interpreting our result. Full Path A had a hold-out F1 of 0.8276, and cyclic encoding alone reached that same value. LIME-guided pruning without the new encoding stayed at the baseline F1 of 0.8138.

That means it would be misleading to say LIME pruning caused the observed hold-out improvement. Its clear contribution was different: pruning reduced the baseline from 22 to 9 predictors without a detectable hold-out F1 loss, while the explanation process helped identify which features to reconsider.

We also did not find a statistically significant predictive advantage for full Path A. So the defensible conclusion is a more compact and interpretable refinement workflow, with a numerical hold-out gain driven by cyclic encoding rather than by LIME alone.
performance:
Thank you. On the final 129-day hold-out, F1 was 0.8138 for the baseline, 0.8276 for LIME-guided Path A, and 0.8219 for gain-guided Path B. Path A classified 104 days correctly, compared with 102 for baseline and 103 for Path B.

Those are small numerical differences. Across 16 expanding-window validation folds, mean F1 was approximately 0.828 to 0.829 for all three models. The paired statistical tests did not find a significant difference.

So I would report the numbers, but not claim that Path A is conclusively more accurate. The stronger result is that refinement produced a smaller model while maintaining comparable predictive performance in this evaluation.
baseline_errors:
Thank you. In the 129-day hold-out, 57 days were dry and 72 were rainy. The baseline correctly identified 43 dry days and 59 rainy days. It made 14 false rain alarms and missed 13 rainy days, for 102 correct predictions overall.

The distinction matters because users may care differently about a missed rainy day and an unnecessary warning. A single accuracy value hides that trade-off. F1 summarizes precision and recall, but it still does not encode a user's specific error costs.

We did not optimize an operational cost function in this paper. To make deployment decisions, we would need to decide which errors matter most and evaluate thresholds against that use case.
f1_choice:
Thank you. Rain made up about 59.9% of the cleaned sample, so accuracy alone would not fully describe how often the classifier misses rain or raises false alarms. F1 combines precision and recall for the rain class at the chosen decision threshold.

AUC-PR adds a view across thresholds that is especially attentive to the positive rain class, while AUC-ROC reports another ranking perspective. We used these measures together because they reveal different aspects of performance.

None is a complete operational metric. F1 does not say whether probabilities are calibrated, and neither F1 nor AUC assigns a cost to a missed rain event. Those questions would need separate analysis before practical use.
significance:
Thank you. The hold-out F1 values differ numerically, but our paired tests did not establish a statistically significant performance difference. For baseline versus Path A, McNemar's p-value was 0.625. After Holm correction, the adjusted p-values for all three model pairs were 1.000, and fold-level Wilcoxon comparisons were also non-significant.

That means the data did not give strong evidence of a difference under these tests. It does not prove the three models are exactly equivalent, and it does not rule out a small real effect that this evaluation lacked power to detect.

So the careful wording is that the refined models had comparable measured performance, with a smaller feature set, rather than a proven accuracy improvement.
mcnemar:
Thank you. The models predicted the same 129 hold-out days, so their errors are paired rather than independent. McNemar's test looks specifically at days where one model was correct and the other was wrong. That is more relevant here than comparing two overall accuracy percentages as though they came from separate samples.

For baseline versus Path A, Path A corrected three baseline errors but introduced one new error. The imbalance of three versus one was small, and the test did not find a significant difference.

McNemar tests disagreement in paired correctness, not the F1 difference directly. It is one piece of evidence alongside the confusion matrices and fold-level score comparisons, with the additional caution that adjacent weather days can be correlated.
cv:
Thank you. We used 16 expanding-window time-series folds. The first training window covered at least three years, and each validation window covered up to 180 calendar days. In total, the folds produced 2,212 pooled predictions from 2013 through 2020.

The essential principle is that a fold trains on earlier dates and tests on later dates. That better reflects a forecasting use case than randomly mixing days. The close mean F1 scores across folds also help show that the small hold-out differences were not consistently large.

However, tuning and feature selection were not fully repeated inside each fold, and one fold overlaps the final hold-out period. A nested design with a separate untouched test period would give a cleaner estimate.
autocorrelation:
Thank you. Rain on one day can be related to rain on the next, so treating all pooled day-level outcomes as independent is a simplifying assumption. That can make a pooled McNemar p-value less secure than it appears.

To check the conclusion from another angle, we compared the 16 fold-level F1 scores using Wilcoxon and paired t-tests. Those comparisons were also non-significant. They do not erase every dependence issue, because the folds share historical training data, but they reduce reliance on a single pooled test.

I would therefore use the p-values as cautious evidence that we did not detect a difference, not as proof of strict equivalence or definitive independence.
shap:
Thank you. The published paper here is about LIME-guided refinement. It mentions a separate TreeSHAP companion analysis, described as under review in the paper, with the same gain-guided Path B comparator.

The presentation reports a SHAP-guided hold-out F1 of 0.8356 and a CV mean F1 of 0.829. Its difference from baseline was also not statistically significant. Those numbers may be useful context, but they are not evidence that this LIME paper itself tested and proved SHAP superior.

I would keep the two studies separate when answering. The conclusion we defend from this paper is about LIME as diagnostic feedback, feature reduction, and the absence of a proven predictive advantage.
case:
Thank you. The 22 December 2020 example is a false negative: both the baseline and Path A missed the next-day light-rain event. Each assigned a rain probability of 0.491, just below the 0.5 decision cutoff.

The explanations differed in form. The baseline LIME account emphasized low relative humidity; Path A expressed a similar dry-air signal through a large temperature–dew point spread. That illustrates how a changed feature representation can change the explanation even when the prediction itself does not improve.

It is one case study, not proof that the explanations are universally faithful or that Path A handles errors better. The broader performance and fidelity questions need aggregate evaluation.
future:
Thank you. I would first redesign the evaluation pipeline so explanation-based feature selection, imputation, and tuning occur using only training data inside each validation fold. I would also give the LIME and gain paths the same candidate-feature pool, which would make their comparison more controlled.

Second, I would preserve exact calendar-day alignment when creating lag features and the next-day target. That would remove the horizon ambiguity introduced by dropping missing rainfall rows.

Finally, I would test multiple BMKG stations and later periods to evaluate transfer beyond Bandung. Hourly nowcasting with radar data is a separate, longer-term project. These steps would strengthen the evidence before claiming operational reliability or generalization.
